title: FCT 14: Ready to Act
description: from insight → to vocation: commissioned as salt and light in the tech world.
content:
**Movement V — Abundant Life & Sending · Day 12**

*Arc: from insight → to vocation: commissioned as salt and light in the tech world.*

*Anchor text: Matthew 5:13-16 · Supporting: Acts 1:8; James 1:22; Matthew 25:14-30; Jeremiah 29:7; Micah 6:8 (refrain — resolution) · Story: Noah, the flood, and the redwoods*

This is the commissioning module. Everything the course has built — the lament, the lenses, the repentance, the reordered loves, the rebuilt commons, the telos of abundant life — now converts to vocation. The FHT course ends with a call to change the culture of technology; the Christian course ends with something older and stronger: a sending.

## Opening — The Refrain Resolves

Read Micah 6:8 one final time, whole: "He has shown you, O mortal, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you? To act justly and to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God." The course has walked its clauses in order — humbly (Module 4), mercy (Module 6), justly (Module 12) — and now they gather into one requirement for one sent people. Pray with 2 Timothy 1:7: *Lord, you have not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-discipline. What you have shown us, we cannot unsee; what you require, we now go to do. Send us.*

## Humane Tech Concepts in View

This module pairs with FHT's *Ready to Act*, the final module of the chain:

- **Recap and call to action** — the core concepts of every FHT module gathered, and the charge to act on them: the technology industry's paradigm can shift, and participants are the ones to shift it.
- **A spirit of service and learning** — change approached with humility, not crusade.
- **Four steps for changing tech culture:** tell your personal story; find collaborators who share the vision; achieve initial small wins that demonstrate impact; champion a new definition of success.
- **Community and movement** — the humane technology ecosystem, partner organizations, and resources for every role and career stage.
- **Mind the Gap, revisited** — the Module 4 exercise returns: has the gap between values and life narrowed?
- **The redwood image** — redwood seeds germinate after fire; tech crises open ground for new growth. Plant seeds now; be ready when the canopy opens.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

1. Synthesize the course into a cohesive Christian framework for engaging and shaping technology, module by module.
2. Articulate technology development and use as Christian vocation — salt and light expressed through work, parenting, and ministry.
3. Craft and deliver a personal testimony of how faith now informs their technology choices and building.
4. Apply the four culture-change steps within an Acts 1:8 pattern of expanding witness — congregation, neighborhood, industry, world.
5. Revisit Mind the Gap and measure movement since Module 4, committing to one next adjustment.
6. Identify their community of ongoing support — Christian tech networks, ecumenical partners, and the broader humane technology movement — and their contribution to it.

## Teaching

### Introduction: Salt, Light, and Doers

We stand where faith intersects the immense power of modern technology, and the course's final word is Jesus' oldest job description: "You are the salt of the earth... You are the light of the world" (Matthew 5:13-16). Our faith compels us not to retreat from the digital realm but to engage it with wisdom, courage, and love — in cyberspace, in the algorithms shaping experience, in the technologies remaking the world. And the standard is James 1:22: "Do not merely listen to the word, and so deceive yourselves. Do what it says." Understanding was never the destination.

### Scripture Engagement

**Matthew 5:13-16 — the anchor.** Salt and light are two distinct modes of witness, and the tech world needs both. Salt works *dissolved and hidden* — preserving and seasoning from inside the dish: the Christian engineer whose presence quietly changes what a team will and won't ship. Light works *visible and raised* — the lamp on its stand, the city on a hill: the community whose alternative practices can be seen from a distance. Note that the city is corporate; the witness Jesus describes is not only individual integrity but a *visible common life* — which is why this course kept insisting on church practice, not just personal habits. And the warning is real: salt can lose its saltiness. Assimilated Christians preserve nothing.

**Matthew 25:14-30 — the talents.** The master entrusts staggering capital and leaves. The servant condemned is not the one who lost money but the one who *buried* it out of fear. We have been entrusted with god-like capabilities — and burying them (retreat, tech-abstinence as identity, cynical disengagement) is the one strategy Jesus explicitly condemns. Venture the talents.

**Acts 1:8 — the deployment pattern.** "You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth" — witness in expanding circles. For digital disciples: your congregation, your neighborhood, your industry, the world. Start where you are; the circles widen on their own schedule.

**Jeremiah 29:7 — building in Babylon.** "Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile... for in its welfare you will find your welfare." We did not choose the platforms of our exile, but the exiles' instructions stand: build houses, plant gardens, seek the city's peace. Digital Babylon is not evacuated; it is gardened.

## Conclusion

We began in lament; we end at a threshold. Carry the vision of technology aligned with Kingdom values; be salt and light whether you ship code, raise children, or shepherd a congregation; stay connected to the community formed here; cultivate digital discipleship as ongoing habit; watch for the redwood openings that crises create; and remain grounded in prayer and Scripture, letting God renew your mind faster than the feeds can shape it. "Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord" (Colossians 3:23-24). Go forth as digital disciples — ready to act, equipped to serve, prepared to lead.

*Closing prayer:* Heavenly Father, thank you for the wisdom you have granted through this journey. Give us courage to act boldly, humility to serve selflessly, and discernment for the landscape ahead. May our work in technology always point to you. In Jesus' name, Amen.

One session remains — not more content, but consecration: tomorrow the cohort reflects, covenants, and commissions one another. **Module 15 — Digital Discipleship Retrospective.**

## Go Deeper

A shelf for the road: John Dyer, *From the Garden to the City* · Andy Crouch, *The Tech-Wise Family* · Tony Reinke, *12 Ways Your Phone Is Changing You* · Cal Newport, *Digital Minimalism* (read through a Christian lens) · Tim Challies, *The Next Story* · Quentin Schultze, *Habits of the High-Tech Heart* · Sutton & Smith, *Redeeming Technology* · Brad J. Kallenberg, *God and Gadgets: Following Jesus in a Technological Age* (2011) · Jacob Shatzer, *Transhumanism and the Image of God* · Ian G. Barbour, *Ethics in an Age of Technology* (1993).
